raw_response:
I’m farming only 10.1 mu, and there are just two people in my house, so I can’t spread myself too thin. For me, wheat-maize is still the safest way. I’ve done this a long time, and around here if wheat is managed steadily and maize goes in quickly after harvest, I can still keep a decent harvest. I have well water, so I’m not fully dependent on rain, but pumping costs money, so I won’t irrigate carelessly. I usually stay close to what has worked on my land, then adjust a little if the crop stand or weather looks off.

For wheat, I’ll sow in early October like usual, using a common local improved variety. I don’t want to cut fertilizer too much because wheat shows it quickly if it runs short, especially after winter. I’ll put most of the phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, then split nitrogen between base and jointing. I expect to irrigate about three times if the season is normal: one after sowing if moisture is short, one at jointing, and one around grain filling depending on rain. For maize, the key is speed. After wheat harvest in June, I’ll get the field turned over fast and plant within a few days. I’ll use hybrid seed, put on base fertilizer, then topdress once around the big bell stage. If summer rain is decent, I may only irrigate once, but if it turns dry I’ll add another. I’m not chasing the highest yield possible. I want a stable crop without spending so much that I leave myself short of cash.
